title: Ibn Battuta leaves Tangier
hookLine: he leaves home alone for the Hajj, and the road keeps going (Rihla)
tomorrow: what did a traveler see on a Friday in Mali?

cards: Travel videos open on a sunrise over a new city, never on the goodbye at the front door. Ibn Battuta's book does it backwards.
Before a single wonder, he describes leaving Tangier: no companion to cheer him, no caravan to join, his parents still living, and a parting so hard that both they and he were stricken with grief.
Why would a travel book begin in tears?

teach.h: A PULL STRONGER THAN THE GRIEF.
teach.b: Because the reason was bigger than the grief, and he wants you to feel both.
In his Rihla, his book of travels, he says he set out alone, moved by a strong pull inside him and a longing he had carried a long time: to visit the holy places, to make the Hajj.
So he steeled himself, he says, to leave his dear ones, and he left home the way birds leave their nests. That picture solves the puzzle. A bird doesn't leave the nest because the nest is bad.
It leaves because it has grown into something that has to fly. The goodbye is in the book because the love was real.

teach.h: FOR WHOEVER CAN FIND A WAY.
teach.b: The Qur'an speaks of the Hajj as a duty owed to God, in Pickthall's words, “for him who can find a way thither.” Ibn Battuta found a way, and paid for it in goodbyes.
The Hajj was his destination, but the road kept going, years of it, through lands he couldn't have pictured from Tangier, and the book was later set down from his telling.
It all begins with one man at the edge of his city, sad and sure at the same time.

how: Muslims setting out for Hajj often visit family to say goodbye and ask forgiveness before they leave; Ibn Battuta's Rihla is read as a classic of Muslim travel writing.

games.q: what does “ibn battuta leaves tangier” mean?
o: a sea battle fought off the coast of Morocco
the moment a traveler set out alone for the Hajj
a sultan's welcome for a traveler coming home

s: Ibn Battuta set out with a group of friends
he says he left alone, with no companion and no caravan to join.
his parents were alive when he left, and the parting grieved them all
both they and he were stricken with sorrow.
his goal at the start was to make the Hajj
a longing to visit the holy places.

games.q: your best friend took a job across the country and keeps saying the move 'isn't a big deal.' what fits Ibn Battuta's opening?
o: it's okay to say it's sad and still go; he did both.
if it were the right move, it wouldn't feel sad.
the sadness is a sign she should turn it down.
games.why: the Rihla starts with real grief at parting and a pull strong enough to go anyway. sadness didn't mean the road was wrong.

practice: Stand up and take a few slow steps toward a door or a window, as if setting out on a long road. With each step, name one small thing that would move a goal of yours forward.
Then come back, sit, and stay with the last one you named.

wordCard.voice: Ibn Battuta leaves Tangier: the opening of his Rihla, a traveler setting out alone for the Hajj, grieving and certain.

orig.note: Arabic: rihla, a journey, and the name for a book of travels like Ibn Battuta's.

carryVoice: What stays with you: alone, on the road, sad and sure at the same time. See you down the road.

sources.ref: Ibn Battuta, Rihla (Tuhfat al-Nuzzar), opening: the departure from Tangier
